questions.explain: Data sovereignty is the principle that data is subject to the laws of the jurisdiction where it resides; residency (storing data in a specific jurisdiction) is one mechanism for achieving it, not the whole concept.
options: They are identical terms
Sovereignty is the principle that data is subject to a jurisdiction's laws; residency is storing data in a specific jurisdiction — one mechanism, not the whole concept
Sovereignty only applies to backups
Residency is about people, sovereignty about databases
questions.q: How does Chapter 26 distinguish data sovereignty from data residency?

questions.explain: A well-meaning DR setup — cross-region snapshot copies or S3 cross-region replication to non-compliant regions — is the most common sovereignty violation, so the DBA must audit the automation.
options: Developers choosing the wrong collation
A well-meaning DR setup copying snapshots/backups to non-compliant regions
Support engineers viewing the portal
Excessive columnstore compression
questions.q: What is the most common data sovereignty violation, according to the chapter?

questions.explain: Each Azure region has a designated pair (usually in the same geography), and failover groups default within the pair — keeping DR inside the sovereignty boundary.
options: Failover groups default within the paired region, keeping DR inside the sovereignty boundary
LTR backups always stay in the primary region
Telemetry never leaves the region
Customer-managed keys are optional
questions.q: Why do Azure paired regions matter for sovereignty?

questions.explain: Control-plane logs, SQL Server audit, and backup/restore logs must be shipped to immutable, retention-locked storage in the compliant region — audit logs that can be modified are not evidence.
options: Keeping logs only for 30 days
Storing logs on the DBA's laptop
Shipping all three log types to immutable, retention-locked storage in the compliant region
Disabling audit to save storage costs
questions.q: What makes audit logs count as compliance evidence?

questions.explain: Vertical partitioning by classification puts personal data in its own tables with restricted access (which also simplifies erasure), while analytics and non-production get tokenized data — the sovereignty problem disappears when the data isn't personal.
options: Encrypting everything with the same key
Isolating regulated/personal data into dedicated tables or databases, and tokenizing data at the boundary
Storing all data in one region regardless of classification
Classifying data once at project start and never again
questions.q: What schema design pattern helps with both residency compliance and the right to erasure?

title: Chapter 26: Data Sovereignty and Residency Compliance
